clue.text: Turned out to be irksome to cheat

parts.note: to con someone is to cheat or swindle them
to vex is to annoy, to be irksome to someone

explanation.surface: Something turned out to be an annoying swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' looks like part of a sentence, 'turned out to be', but it is the definition: a shape bulging outwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A convex surface bulges outwards, curving out like the outside of a sphere.

clue.text: Trend's about level

definitions.note: read as 'trend is', the 's being a link

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
to raze a building is to level it to the ground

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a fashion is roughly flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A craze is a short-lived fashion, a passing enthusiasm everyone follows.

clue.text: Erotic writer and original sinner hot from Sin City

parts.note: Anais Nin wrote celebrated erotica
Eve ate the forbidden fruit in Genesis, the first sin
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A racy author and the first sinful woman arrive fresh from a notoriously wicked city.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR text has 'not', a misreading of 'hot', which supplies H. NINEVEH is the Assyrian city condemned for its wickedness in the Book of Jonah.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Assyrian capital was denounced by the prophets as a byword for wickedness, a biblical city of sin.

clue.text: Insular type to buck up hero with honour

indicators.note: buck as in a bucking horse throwing things about, so the letters of the words before are jumbled

parts.note: the OBE, Order of the British Empire, is a British honour

explanation.surface: A narrow-minded islander tries to cheer up a decorated hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to buck' makes EUROPH from the letters of UP HERO; 'buck up' reads as 'cheer up', hiding the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dislikes the European continent is often called insular, wary of all things beyond Britain's shores.

clue.text: Calculator used in French exam down under?

indicators.note: the exam word sits within the word for Australia

parts.note: Down Under is a nickname for Australia, abbreviated AUS
the bac, short for baccalaureat, is the French school-leaving exam

explanation.surface: A counting frame is allowed in a French exam held in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down under' with a question mark hints at the location of the exam; 'used' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame of beads on rods was the original counting device, used for arithmetic long before electronics.

clue.text: Second to survive explosion

parts.note: B is the second letter, as in second class or B-grade
to last is to survive or endure

explanation.surface: A second person somehow lives through a bomb going off.
explanation.definitionFit: A blast is the rush of air and noise from a detonation.

clue.text: Sauce to feature prominently in processed food

indicators.note: the starring word goes inside the cow's food

parts.note: cud is food a cow brings back up to chew again, so it has been processed once
to star is to feature prominently, as in a film

explanation.surface: A dressing is the highlight of some ready meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'processed food' suggests factory meals, but it is the cow's chewed CUD.
explanation.definitionFit: Custard is a sweet pouring sauce of milk, eggs and sugar served with puddings.

clue.text: Feeling the punishment one received

indicators.note: the punishment takes in the numeral, as if receiving it

parts.note: a sentence is the punishment handed down by a court
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone describes how they felt about the penalty a person was given.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentience is the capacity to feel and perceive, awareness through sensation.

clue.text: Girl comes in to sample skin treatment centre

indicators.note: the girl enters the word for sample, sitting inside it

parts.note: to try something is to sample it
Anne is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman visits a salon to try out a beauty treatment for the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skin treatment centre' reads like a beauty spa; the skins are animal hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A tannery is a works where animal hides are cured into leather.

clue.text: Temporary death

explanation.definitionFit: A passing fancy is temporary or fleeting; one's passing is a gentle word for dying.

clue.text: Lawrence inverted (and Bar stow included) in gymnastic feat

indicators.note: the bracketed words are placed within the writer's initials
the initials are turned upside down, reading in reverse order

parts.note: D H Lawrence, the novelist, gives his initials
Stan Barstow, the Yorkshire novelist, gives his first name

explanation.surface: A novelist, upside down with another writer tucked in, performs an acrobatic move.
explanation.walkthrough: Stan Barstow and D H Lawrence were both English novelists of working-class life; the print splits Barstow in two. 'inverted' also nicely pictures someone upside down on their hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Balancing upside down on the hands is a standard gymnastics move.

clue.text: JCB, say, makes unsubtle infiltrator

parts.note: heavy-handed is unsubtle, so heavy means lacking delicacy
a plant is a spy placed inside an organisation

explanation.surface: A digger turns out to be a clumsy undercover agent.
explanation.walkthrough: JCB is a British maker of diggers, and the name is used for any mechanical excavator.
explanation.definitionFit: Excavators, bulldozers and cranes are grouped together as large construction machinery, of which a JCB digger is an example.

clue.text: Novelist not quite out of order

indicators.note: the word falls just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: something amiss is wrong or out of order

explanation.surface: A writer's behaviour is described as slightly improper.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Amis and his son Martin are both well-known British novelists.

clue.text: Lout loves bedding to be turned over

indicators.note: the straw is flipped round, read in reverse order

parts.note: hay is used as bedding for animals
love is zero in tennis, and an O looks like zero, so two loves are OO

explanation.surface: A thug likes to have his mattress flipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be turned over' sits by 'bedding', so only the straw flips, as a mattress might.
explanation.definitionFit: A yahoo is a coarse, brutish person, from the beast-men in Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Detectives' parasite proves an exemplar

parts.note: Scotland Yard, the London police headquarters, stands for its detectives, so 'Detectives'' gives the Yard's
a tick is a bloodsucking parasite

explanation.surface: A police force's pest turns out to be a model case.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a standard by which others are measured, a model or benchmark.

clue.text: Naughty nineties" say conservationists

parts.note: the nineties are a ten-year period, an example of one
the NT, the National Trust, is a British conservation charity

explanation.surface: A heritage group comments on the risque era of the 1890s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks the nineties as an example. The 'Naughty Nineties' was the decadent 1890s, so the definition is built into the surface phrase. The NT looks after historic houses and countryside in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent describes self-indulgent, morally lax behaviour, fittingly wicked in a fun way.

clue.text: Tea-folk receive the sign of the lizard

parts.note: cha is a slang word for tea

indicators.note: the people take in the star sign, holding it inside

parts.note: folk are people, men
Leo is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Tea drinkers are given a lizard emblem.
explanation.definitionFit: A chameleon is a colour-changing reptile, a kind of lizard with a long sticky tongue.

clue.text: Growing areas without a coin

indicators.note: the areas word goes without, losing, the following letter

parts.note: acres are areas of land
a cent is a small coin

explanation.surface: Some cultivated fields lack any money.
explanation.definitionFit: Crescent comes from the Latin for increasing, as a waxing moon swells; heraldry uses it for a moon that is getting bigger.

clue.text: Blade that's converted Saul accepting sporting trophy

indicators.note: the rearranged name takes in the award, holding it
Saul famously converted on the road to Damascus; here his letters are converted into a new order

parts.note: a cap is awarded to a player chosen for a national team

explanation.surface: A biblical convert accepts a sports award, which sounds like a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Saul's Damascus conversion; here 'converted' just jumbles his name, which 'accepting' then wraps round the trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: The scapula is the shoulder blade, the flat triangular bone at the back of the shoulder.

clue.text: Passage is in the drink

indicators.note: the little word sits inside the beer

parts.note: ale is a drink, beer

explanation.surface: A stretch of text is soaked in beer.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a walkway between rows of seats or shelves.

clue.text: Jumper's first course

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who starts or jumps in surprise is a starter; a starter is the opening dish of a meal.

clue.text: A sloth's travelling west to the east

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means reading from right to left

parts.note: the ai is a three-toed sloth, so the sloth's gives that word plus S

explanation.surface: A lazy animal heads west to reach the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'travelling west' turns AIS into SIA. 'Sloth's' is the ai's, plus an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the continent long known in the West as the East or the Orient.

clue.text: A ballet dancer let out to organise light fittings

indicators.note: the three letters are let out of the dancer's words, removed from the pool
the remaining letters are organised into a new order

explanation.surface: A dancer is released to arrange the lamps.
explanation.walkthrough: Take LET out of A BALLET DANCER and 'to organise' the remaining ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A candelabra is a branched holder for several candles or lights.

clue.text: Socialist without firm convictions

definitions.note: plural, while a credo is a single set of beliefs

indicators.note: here meaning outside: the firm's letters wrap around the political one

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
red is a common term for a socialist or communist

explanation.surface: A left-winger is described as lacking firm beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking, so the firm surrounds the socialist.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement of beliefs, what one holds firmly to be true.

clue.text: Ambassador stifled by funny old cold

indicators.note: the diplomat is smothered within the word for strange

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or funny
HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: A diplomat is choked by a strange chill.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is an old word for the watery discharge of a head cold.

clue.text: Bolt securing centre of Gulf Stream

indicators.note: the bolt holds the middle letters inside it

parts.note: a rivet is a metal bolt

indicators.note: the central letters of the word for a bay are taken

explanation.surface: A fastener holds part of the warm Atlantic current in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of' takes UL from GULF; the Gulf Stream is the misleading picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A rivulet is a small stream or brook.

clue.text: Unconverted roast chicken?

parts.note: to heat food is to roast or cook it
a hen is a chicken

explanation.surface: A recipe asks whether this roast bird is uncooked.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture suggests 'unconverted' means raw; it means not having adopted a religion.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone outside a faith, not won over to the religion of the speaker.

clue.text: Endless penner of odes on a silent star

indicators.note: the poet loses his final letter

parts.note: John Keats wrote famous odes such as To a Nightingale

explanation.surface: A poet with no ending turns to a star of silent cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: Buster Keaton was a deadpan comic star of the silent film era.

clue.text: An operation in the barber's county

parts.note: a trim is a light haircut done at the barber's

explanation.surface: A haircut is offered at the barber's somewhere in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: ANTRIM is a county of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrim is one of the six historic counties of Northern Ireland.
